newsitem.title: HUNGARY: Hungary home finance heats up with new law planned.
newsitem.headline: Hungary home finance heats up with new law planned.

text.p: Hungary's housing finance market is about to be shaken up by a German-modelled building society scheme that the industry says should pull home construction and renovation out of the doldrums.
But major banking and insurance groups forming alliances to enter the market say they must await parliamentary approval of the enabling legislation to know exactly what to expect.

"It's not in force yet, it's still a draft which has been approved by the government but not yet by the parliament," said Lajos Csepi, who is in charge of developing strategies for OTP Bank, Hungary's biggest commercial bank, to enter the new market.
"But the draft says that the law must enter into force on the first of January next year, and that is what we are now preparing for," Csepi added.
Hungary built a paltry 20,000 to 30,000 new houses or flats last year, which experts say is below the necessary replacement level in a country of more than 10 million.
But a staggering 90 percent of Hungarian homes are privately owned, almost double the level in wealthy Germany, and that is what sparks interest in the new financing plan.

"What you can say is Hungary definitely has a demand for owning your own home -- to live within your own four walls," said Hannes Buchhaus, who is helping set up a building society called Lakaskassza.
The new building society is 52 percent owned by EA Generali AG of Vienna, Hungary's Providencia insurance group and Generali Budapest.
The other 48 percent is held by a group which includes Hungary's Postabank and Creditanstalt's Hungarian subsidiary, Buchhaus said.

A third powerful player in the equation is Bausparkasse Schwaebisch Hall, Germany's leading building society, which has teamed up with Hungary's cooperative banks, giving it direct access to hundreds of towns and villages.

Nobody knows for sure who will come out on top in a market that could be worth tens of millions of dollars a year, but clearly OTP, which has had a monopoly on Hungarian home financing, has the most to lose.

"The bank itself is in a monopolistic situation on this market so the bank generally is not happy for that," Csepi said. "But the general director and the management understood this must happen and there is no other way but to establish a buidling society or other banks...will attract the clients."
Under the existing system, prospective Hungarian homeowners enter into a contractual plan that after a few years of modest savings entitles them to government-subsidised housing loans.
The system, a hangover from the country's recent communist past, all told costs the government an estimated 90 billion forints ($600 million) a year, bank officials said.

Under the new plan, clients would make savings deposits for a period of four years and the government would subsidise those deposits. Under one version, the government would give a subsidy of 30 percent of the amount deposited, up to a maximum of 36,000 forints ($240) a year. Several family members could save at the same time so substantial funds would accumulate.

The plan cuts the government contribution drastically, to an estimated 12 billion forints ($80 million) annually, according to some estimates. And it puts the emphasis on saving in advance instead of clients expecting government assistance after they have contracted huge debts.

"The philosophy of this draft says that before you make any transaction you must prepare yourself for it. You must collect a big amount of money in order to initiate it in a successful manner," Csepi said.

The banks and insurers who offer the programme stand to make a tidy profit in the first few years, when all the money is flowing into the accounts and nothing is being paid out. But the government has set a hefty reserve figure of 10 percent, which is well above the three percent international standard for building societies, bank officials said.

In addition, the societies are taking a gamble that the plan will catch on with the Hungarian public. If there is a big payout after the first four years, but no new custom coming in, the buildings societies could be in trouble, officials added.

Buchhaus said that if the experience of Austria is anything to go by, Hungary should gain all around. He said that for a government subsidy of three billion Austrian schillings in 1995, the housing industry generated 51 billion in revenues, and indirect taxes from that were 14.2 billion schillings.
"There will be more domestic employment through an expanding industry (in Hungary)," Buchhaus said.

"And -- one more feature --- the societies will help the building industry do things properly and legally," he added, referring to estimates that a third of Hungary's economic activity is done in the black or "grey" markets, to avoid paying taxes.
"I think it will be one of the most important macroeconomic businesses for the Hungarian population," Buchhaus said.
